mcqs.question: A profile field renders `<input value={profile?.email} onChange={e => setEmail(e.target.value)} />`. `profile` is `undefined` until the fetch resolves. When the response lands, React logs 'A component is changing an uncontrolled input to be controlled' and the email the user typed before that is replaced by the server value. Which change keeps the field controlled from the first render?
options: Pass `value={profile?.email}` together with `defaultValue=''`, so the field has a value while the request is pending.
Pass `value={profile?.email ?? ''}` and keep `onChange` writing the new string into state synchronously.
Pass `value={profile?.email}` and key the input by the profile id, so React remounts it when data arrives.
Pass `defaultValue={profile?.email}` and copy the incoming email into local state on every render.
mcqs.explanation: A text input's mode is decided by whether `value` is a string, and React does not let it change over the input's lifetime: the docs' troubleshooting entry for this warning says a controlled input must always receive a string, that `value={undefined}` followed by a string is precisely the uncontrolled-to-controlled change, and that API-sourced values belong behind `value={someValue ?? ''}` (https://react.dev/reference/react-dom/components/input#im-getting-an-error-a-component-is-changing-an-uncontrolled-input-to-be-controlled). The strongest distractor is option 0: `value` plus `defaultValue` looks like belt and braces, but while `value` is undefined the input is still uncontrolled and `defaultValue` is only its initial value, so the same switch happens when the response lands and the user's typing is overwritten. Option 2 remounts the field, which loses the caret and any local state without making the mode stable, and option 3 leaves the field uncontrolled forever while overwriting the user's input with the prop on every render.

mcqs.question: In `<Tabs><Tabs.List/><Tabs.Panel/></Tabs>`, the selected tab lives in the `Tabs` owner and the parts read it from context. Why is the owner the right place for it?
options: Because a context value reaches the parts without re-rendering them when the selection changes.
Because the tab and its panel must agree on one selected value, and the owner is their closest common ancestor.
Because the parts can then find each other by position in the tree instead of carrying generated ids.
Because each `Tabs.Tab` can then keep its own selected flag and stay independent of the list.
mcqs.explanation: Lifting shared state to the closest common parent is react.dev's rule for components that must change together: one source of truth makes the tab's `aria-selected` and the panel's visibility derive from the same value, so they cannot disagree (https://react.dev/learn/sharing-state-between-components). The strongest distractor is option 0: context is a delivery mechanism, not a render optimization — every consumer re-renders when the context value changes, so the reason to lift is coordination, not render count. Option 2 is the position-based shortcut that breaks the moment a tab is conditionally rendered or reordered, and it does not remove generated ids, because `aria-controls` and `aria-labelledby` still need real references. Option 3 restores the bug that lifting fixes: two sources of truth that drift, with the visual tab and the shown panel pointing at different content.

mcqs.question: Which requirement is part of a genuinely modal dialog implementation?
options: Only add `aria-modal=true` to the dialog element
Leave the invoking button focused behind the dialog
Keep Tab and Shift+Tab within the dialog and restore focus on close
Make the backdrop the only way to close it
mcqs.explanation: The APG modal pattern contains the dialog's Tab sequence, moves focus inside on open, and normally returns focus to the invoker on close. Option 0 fails because ARIA does not implement inertness; option 3 excludes the required visible close-button pattern.

mcqs.question: An editable combobox opens a listbox of suggestions while the user types. Where does DOM focus live as Up/Down move the highlight?
options: On the highlighted option, which receives DOM focus as the arrows move.
On the listbox container, using roving tabindex across its options.
On the input, which names the active option via `aria-activedescendant`.
On the input, with the active option conveyed by a CSS highlight only.
mcqs.explanation: APG keeps DOM focus on the combobox and moves the assistive-technology focus inside the listbox with `aria-activedescendant`, so typing keeps working while the arrow keys walk the options (https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/combobox/). The strongest distractor is option 1: roving tabindex is the correct model for menus and toolbars, and porting it into an editable field is the classic failure — the options become Tab stops, Tab no longer leaves the field, and the arrows have to fight the browser's caret movement. Option 0 breaks the same invariant more directly: pulling DOM focus out of the input hides the caret and interrupts the string being typed. Option 3 looks harmless, but the highlight then lives only in CSS, so nothing in the accessibility tree names the active option and a screen-reader user hears no change at all.

mcqs.question: A search box sends a request per debounced query and aborts the previous one. On a slow network a user types `lon`, then `lond`, and the list finally shows results for `lon`. Which change addresses the cause?
options: Raise the debounce to 500 ms, so the shorter query is never sent while the user is typing.
Abort the previous request and swallow `AbortError`, since an abort makes a stale response impossible.
Tag each request and apply a response only while its tag is still the latest, because abort is best effort.
Clear the options on every keystroke, so nothing stale is on screen when the results arrive.
mcqs.explanation: `abort()` stops work, it does not undo a response that already left the server or one that resolved just before the signal fired, so the race has to be closed on arrival: capture a request id per query, increment it on each new query, and drop any response whose id is no longer current — the step the bank calls the one candidates skip and then debug for an hour. The strongest distractor is option 1: it is the right first half and the wrong conclusion, because treating the abort as a guarantee leaves a late response free to land on top of newer results; swallowing `AbortError` only keeps an expected cancellation out of the UI, it does not decide who may write to state. Option 0 hides the race behind timing instead of closing it — a slow proxy reproduces it at any debounce length — and option 3 only empties the list while loading, so the late response repopulates it after the newer results arrived.

mcqs.question: A 50,000-row log table mounts every row, wraps each row in `React.memo`, and is still slow. Rewriting it with windowing fixes it. Which mechanism is doing the work?
options: Memoized rows skip re-rendering, so the whole tree is built once instead of on every keystroke.
Only the visible window plus overscan is mounted, so DOM and reconciliation cost track the viewport, not the dataset.
Rows outside the viewport stay mounted but get `display: none`, so the browser skips their layout and paint.
Rows arrive one page at a time, so the component never holds more than a page of data in memory.
mcqs.explanation: Windowing makes the mounted element count proportional to the viewport: the visible rows plus a small overscan buffer, with an empty spacer standing in for the rest so the scrollbar and the scroll position stay honest. What hurt was 50,000 live DOM nodes and the reconciliation that walks them, and that is the quantity the rewrite shrinks. The strongest distractor is option 2: `display: none` is a real technique that takes hidden rows out of layout and paint, but React still creates, diffs and commits all 50,000 elements and the browser still parses and stores them — the work stays proportional to the dataset, so the page keeps stalling. Option 0 removes repeated renders but not the initial build or the node count, and it does nothing when row props change. Option 3 describes pagination, a data-layer decision: it bounds the dataset per view, and any page large enough to hold 50,000 rows is exactly the case that still needs windowing.

mcqs.question: A paginated table keeps `?page=` in the URL. The user is on page 4, then narrows a status filter so the response has one page of 12 rows. What should happen?
options: Keep `page=4`, render the empty state, and let 'No results' stand because the filter did match fewer rows.
Clamp the page to the new range, or reset it when the filter changed, so the URL never names a missing page.
Keep `page=4` in the URL but render the last page's rows, so the user keeps their position and still sees data.
Disable the filter controls while `page > 1`, so the page can never become invalid in the first place.
mcqs.explanation: An invalid page is prevented where the page is changed, not inside the table: the table renders whatever page it is handed, and the owner clamps against the range the response reports (`hasNext`, a total, or a cursor) whenever a filter or a page size shrinks the range. The strongest distractor is option 0: 'No results' is indistinguishable from 'your filter matched nothing', so the user concludes the filter is broken and removes it — the empty state has to be reserved for a genuinely empty result set, not for a page that fell out of range. Option 2 keeps the view plausible but makes the URL lie, so a shared or restored link shows something other than the page it names. Option 3 gates the input instead of fixing the state, and Back/Forward or a pasted link still lands on page 4.

mcqs.question: A hero carousel rotates automatically on page load. Which behavior must it ship with?
options: A stop/start rotation button, pausing on focus or hover, that never restarts on its own.
A stop/start rotation button, but the timer restarts once focus and the pointer have both left.
A visible countdown to the next slide, after which rotation continues unconditionally.
Rotation that begins only after the user presses Next once, so the first slide is always read.
mcqs.explanation: APG requires a rotation control whose label switches between 'Stop slide rotation' and 'Start slide rotation', rotation that stops when keyboard focus enters the carousel and does not restart unless the user asks for it, and a pause while the pointer hovers; WCAG 2.2.2 separately requires a pause/stop/hide mechanism for auto-updating content that starts by itself (https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/carousel/, https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#pause-stop-hide). The strongest distractor is option 1: the auto-resume timer is what most implementations ship, and it turns control into a temporary pause, so a screen-reader user who paused by focusing is moved to a new slide mid-sentence. Option 2 informs without giving control — a countdown is not a pause mechanism — and option 3 still rotates without a control and without honoring focus.

mcqs.question: A modal dialog, an editable combobox and a menu button each carry their own effect with focus capture, Tab handling and Escape. You are extracting the shared part. Which split keeps all three correct?
options: One `usePopup` that moves focus inside, traps Tab and closes on Escape, parameterized by the popup's role.
A boundary/restore/cleanup hook, plus per-widget config for where focus goes and whether Tab may leave.
One hook that only exposes the popup ref and lets each widget write its own key handlers and focus loop.
One hook per widget that shares just the `document.activeElement` snapshot and the restore call.
mcqs.explanation: Share the mechanics, keep the semantics: where focus was, where it goes on open, how it comes back, and how listeners are cleaned up are common; whether focus may leave at all is not. A modal dialog cycles Tab inside, an editable combobox lets Tab leave while the arrows drive a listbox through `aria-activedescendant`, and a menu button closes the menu and moves on (https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/dialog-modal/, https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/combobox/, https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/menu-button/). The strongest distractor is option 0: it is the DRY-looking answer, and it encodes the dialog's containment as universal, so the hook swallows Tab and breaks the combobox. Option 2 goes the other way and shares almost nothing, so every widget re-implements the trap and the cleanup bugs return; option 3 keeps the restore but still duplicates the boundary and dismissal policy, which is where the divergent bugs live.

mcqs.question: A sortable, paginated table stores its view in the query string so a link reproduces what the user saw. Which set belongs there?
options: `page`, `sort` and the toolbar filters, so Back/Forward and a shared link restore the same view.
`page` only, because filters are transient UI and a shared link should open the unfiltered table.
Every state value, including the pending flag and the loaded rows, so a refresh can skip the request.
`page`, `sort` and filters, rewritten on each filter keystroke so the URL is never stale.
mcqs.explanation: The URL is the shareable, navigable projection of the view: page, sort and user-meaningful filters belong there because they describe what is on screen, and Back/Forward then restores it; transient flags and fetched data do not. The strongest distractor is option 3: writing on every keystroke fills the history with one entry per character, so a single Back press undoes one letter, and the URLs people copy are half-typed queries — write on commit, or debounced with a replace instead of a push. Option 1 defeats the purpose, because a link that opens a different view than the one the user is looking at cannot be shared to reproduce a report. Option 2 turns the URL into a cache, which makes it long, stale, and a place where row data that may be personal ends up in browser history.

mcqs.question: In D3, `selection.data(rows)` joins by index. What does passing a key function — `selection.data(rows, d => d.id)` — change?
options: Elements are matched to their datum by identity, so a re-sorted dataset moves existing nodes instead of rebinding them.
The DOM is reordered to follow the data, so a sort no longer needs an explicit `selection.order()` call.
Datums that share a key collapse into one element, so two rows with the same id never render twice.
Each element receives its key as a stable `id` attribute, so CSS selectors keep matching the same datum.
mcqs.explanation: A key function replaces the default join-by-index with a match on a computed key, which is object constancy: the node that carried datum A keeps datum A when the array is re-sorted, so it can be moved or transitioned instead of silently receiving someone else's values (https://d3js.org/d3-selection/joining). The strongest distractor is option 1: keys decide which datum a node carries, not where the node sits, and the docs are explicit that update and enter follow data order while the document may not, so `selection.order()` or `selection.sort()` is still required after a re-sort. Option 2 inverts the documented behavior: duplicate data go to the enter selection and duplicate elements go to the exit selection, so duplicates produce extra elements rather than being merged. Option 3 confuses the join key with the HTML `id`: the datum is stored on the node's `__data__` property and nothing writes the key into an attribute, so a CSS selector cannot follow identity.

mcqs.question:
A controlled email field renders `{error &&

{error}

}`. Which wiring gets that message to a screen reader without moving the user's cursor?
options: Focus the input whenever `error` changes, so the field is announced together with its message.
Set `aria-errormessage={errorId}` on the input and unmount the message while the user is typing, to keep announcements quiet.
Set `aria-invalid` from the current validity and reference `errorId` in `aria-describedby` only while the message is rendered.
Copy the message into the input's `placeholder` and add a `title` on the wrapping element.
mcqs.explanation: A description needs two things at once: a truthful state flag and an id reference to text that is actually in the accessibility tree. `aria-invalid` carries validity; `aria-describedby` points at the rendered message, so it is read on demand and again when focus returns to the field, and nothing touches the caret (https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/error-identification.html). The strongest distractor is option 1: `aria-errormessage` is real ARIA, but it is only a pointer to an element that must exist and be exposed, so unmounting the text mid-typing leaves the reference dangling and silent. Option 0 destroys the caret position on every keystroke and interrupts typing, and option 3 hides the text from assistive tech while removing the field's visible name as soon as the user types.

mcqs.question: In a React list keyed by `item.id`, a keyboard user activates `Move item down` on the third of five rows. Which follow-up does the reorder actually require?
options: Nothing extra: the rows are keyed by id, so the focused button keeps its identity across the reorder.
The array is swapped and focus moves to the first row, so the user can Tab back into the list from a known place.
The array is swapped and every Move button is disabled until the user leaves and re-enters the list, which prevents accidental repeated moves.
The array is swapped, focus returns to the moved item (or its logical successor), and a status message announces the new position.
mcqs.explanation: A reorder is a state change plus a focus and announcement contract: the moved item keeps the user's attention, and a polite live region reports where it landed, which is the only feedback a screen-reader user gets (https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/listbox/examples/listbox-rearrangeable/, https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/status-messages.html). The strongest distractor is option 0: keys preserve reconciliation identity, not focus. The row can still remount through a conditional parent or an index-keyed sibling, and a button that becomes `disabled` at the new boundary blurs, dropping focus to `<body>`. Even when focus survives, nothing is announced, so the user cannot tell whether the move happened. Option 1 throws away the user's place, and option 2 strands focus on a control that just became unavailable.

mcqs.question: A help icon reveals a one-line definition. Which implementation lets a keyboard-only user hear it?
options: Show it on hover only; keyboard users read the same text from a `title` attribute on the icon.
Show it on focus as well as hover, reference it with `aria-describedby` while it is open, keep DOM focus on the trigger, and dismiss on Escape.
Give the tooltip `tabindex="0"` so Tab reaches the text and Escape can dismiss it from inside.
Show it on focus and move focus into the tooltip so the screen reader reads the whole string.
mcqs.explanation: The tooltip pattern is defined by two things: the trigger points at the text with `aria-describedby`, and focus never leaves the trigger, so the description is read without a mode change; Escape dismisses it while the user keeps their place (https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/tooltip/). The strongest distractor is option 2: making the text focusable is the classic accessibility fix, but a tooltip widget does not receive focus. The extra Tab stop leads to a non-interactive popup, and once the panel is focusable and interactive it is a non-modal dialog, not a tooltip, and has to be built as one. Option 0 fails because `title` is not shown on keyboard focus and is inconsistently exposed; option 3 breaks the focus-stays-on-trigger rule and claims tooltip semantics for a dialog interaction.

mcqs.question: In a four-step form, step 2 has one invalid field and the user presses Next. Which behavior keeps state, validation, and focus coherent?
options: Validate step 2 only, stay on step 2, associate each message with its field, and focus the first invalid control.
Validate all four steps, advance to step 3, and mark the invalid field so the user can come back to it.
Advance to step 3 and show an error summary there, since the user has already signalled intent to move on.
Disable Next until every field in the step is valid, so an invalid step can never be submitted.
mcqs.explanation: A step transition is a guarded state update: validate the step being left, refuse the transition while it fails, tie each message to its control, and put focus on the first invalid field so the announcement has a target (https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/error-identification.html). Going back is the mirror case, and it must not validate, or the user gets trapped. The strongest distractor is option 3: disabling Next looks safer, but it removes the only event that can explain why the step will not advance, so nothing is announced and the user hunts for the cause. Option 1 validates fields the user never visited and moves them away from the problem; option 2 detaches the message from the field it describes.

scenarios.prompt: Machine-coding round (45 min). This city picker ships with QA notes: on a slow connection, typing `lon` and then `lond` ends with the list for `lon`; the network tab shows one request per keystroke; NVDA reads the field as 'City, edit text' and says nothing when the arrows move the highlight; and after a mouse pick the next Tab starts from the top of the page. Keep the input focused and the `value` + `onChange` contract, then fix the race, the request volume, the ARIA wiring and the index-based highlight.
rubric: Closes the race with both halves: abort in cleanup plus a request token that discards a response whose id is no longer current.
Debounces the request (not the input) with the timer cleared in cleanup, keeps real errors visible and drops `AbortError` deliberately.
Wires the combobox contract: `role=combobox`, `aria-expanded`, `aria-controls`, and `aria-activedescendant` pointing at a rendered option id.
Tracks the active option by id and clamps at both ends, instead of storing an index into an array that gets replaced.
Keeps focus in the input on mouse selection, commits without re-searching the label, and covers Escape plus loading, empty and error states.

scenarios.prompt: Machine-coding round (45 min). This hand-rolled modal passes its own demo and fails review: with the dialog open, Tab walks out of it into the page behind; a screen reader in browse mode still reads the product list behind it; after closing, focus is on `<body>` and the next Tab starts at the top of the page; and Escape stops closing the dialog as soon as focus is on the Close button. Say what the code actually does, explain why `aria-modal` delivers none of it, and write the version you would merge.
rubric: Predicts the behavior correctly: focus on the overlay, no containment, Escape only while the overlay itself is the event target.
Explains `aria-modal` as an assertion with no inertness behind it, tying the browse-mode leak to the missing `inert` or `aria-hidden` on the page.
Traces the lost focus to the missing opener capture, and the broken Escape to the `target === currentTarget` guard.
Ships native `<dialog>` with `showModal()`, `cancel`/`close` listeners and no `tabindex` on the dialog; states the focus placement and restore behavior.
Names the hand-rolled fallback pieces (capture/restore, inert shell, boundary cycling, top-most Escape ownership) and how to verify with keyboard and screen reader.

scenarios.prompt: Machine-coding round (45 min). This fixed-height virtual list renders the first screen correctly and then breaks: scrolling past it shows blank space while the scrollbar keeps moving; Tab reaches the scroll container but no row; a screen-reader user hears nothing when the highlight moves; and a selection set from outside never scrolls into view. Predict what the positioning math produces, keep the DOM small, and add the keyboard and selection contract.
rubric: Fixes the offset: rows are positioned by absolute index, `(first + i) * rowHeight` or a wrapper translated by `first * rowHeight`, so the window paints where the viewport is.
Keys rows by `row.id` and keeps selection by id, so a shifted window never rebinds a mounted node to another record.
Adds a real keyboard path: one roving tab stop, ArrowUp/ArrowDown/Home/End, Enter or Space to select, not mouse-only clicks.
Wires listbox semantics (`role=listbox`, `role=option`, `aria-selected`) and scrolls a selection set from outside into view without requiring the row to be mounted.
Clamps the window to the dataset, uses overscan as a buffer, and states the fixed-height limit and the find-in-page trade-off.

scenarios.prompt: Machine-coding round (45 min). This bar chart runs `render(data)` on every refresh and has three defects: the chart is blank until the second render; after a re-sort the bars' hover tooltips still name the old label and value while their heights are already new; and after filtering one series out, the wrong bar disappears. Predict what the enter/update/exit chain does, explain each symptom from the code, and rewrite the join.
scenarios.modelAnswer:
Run the chain once, on the first call. `svg.selectAll('rect.bar')` matches nothing, so `data(data)` returns an empty update selection with every datum in enter. `enter().append('rect')` creates the rectangles with their class and a `<title>` child — and that is all, because the chained `bars.transition().attr(...)` below is applied to the update selection, which is still empty. SVG rects default to width and height 0, so the chart is blank. On the second call the update selection holds the rects and the geometry finally arrives, which is the 'blank until the next refresh' symptom. The fix is not a `merge()` at the end; it is to give enter its geometry too, or to join enter and update and apply one chain to the result.

The stale tooltips are enter-only configuration. The `<title>` text is written once, when the node is created, with the datum that node had at that moment. A re-sort never touches it, because nothing in the update path selects the title, so the native tooltip keeps naming the old label and value while the height, computed from the current datum, is already new. Text and attributes both have to be re-applied to the merged selection on every render — a rule that generalizes to every data-driven label in the chart.

The wrong bar disappearing is the index join. Without a key function the join is positional, so with one datum fewer, elements 0..n-2 take the new data and the tail element exits: whichever series was filtered out, the last DOM rect is the one removed, and every remaining rect changes height. The node never carried an identity that could have said 'this one left'.

The rewrite keeps the function shape and fixes the model:

```ts
function render(data: Point[]) {
  x.domain(data.map(d => d.label));
  y.domain([0, d3.max(data, d => d.value) ?? 0]);

  const bars = svg
    .selectAll<SVGRectElement, Point>('rect.bar')
    .data(data, d => d.id);                        // identity, not position

  const merged = bars.join(                       // one path for enter and update
    enter =>
      enter
        .append('rect')
        .attr('class', 'bar')
        .attr('x', d => x(d.label) ?? 0)
        .attr('y', height)
        .attr('width', x.bandwidth())
        .attr('height', 0)
        .call(sel => sel.append('title')),
    update => update,
    exit =>
      exit
        .transition()
        .duration(200)
        .attr('y', height)
        .attr('height', 0)
        .remove()
  );

  merged.select('title').text(d => d.label + ': ' + d.value);

  merged
    .transition()
    .duration(300)
    .attr('x', d => x(d.label) ?? 0)
    .attr('y', d => y(d.value))
    .attr('width', x.bandwidth())
    .attr('height', d => height - y(d.value));

  merged.order();                                 // keys do not reorder the DOM
}
```

`selection.order()` is not decoration: a key function decides which datum a node carries, not where the node sits, so after a re-sort the document order can disagree with the data order — the d3 docs say so explicitly, and the bars would tab and read in the old sequence. Accessibility is a separate obligation: rects are not reachable, so the SVG gets a takeaway label and a real table beside it, which is the version a screen-reader user can read values from. With time left I would check the empty-array case, where `d3.max` returns undefined and the domain collapses, and whether the first render should skip the transition entirely.
rubric: Predicts the first call correctly: the update selection is empty, so enter-only rects never get geometry and the chart stays blank until the next render.
Attributes the stale tooltips to enter-only `<title>` configuration rather than to the join, and refreshes the text on the merged selection.
Explains the vanishing bar as the index join (the tail exits) and adds a key function for object constancy.
Puts enter and update on one path (`join` or `merge`) with transitions inside each branch, and calls `selection.order()` after a re-sort.
Keeps accessibility separate (SVG label plus a table fallback) and names the empty-data/domain edge case.

scenarios.prompt: Machine-coding round (45 min). This field renders, validates, and reports changes, but it fails a keyboard and screen-reader pass. Keep the parent contract (`value` + `onChange`), add the missing label and error associations, choose when validation should run, and state how the message is announced.
scenarios.modelAnswer:
I would name the four defects before touching code, because each one maps to a different obligation. The `<span>` is not a label: the input has no accessible name except the placeholder, and the placeholder disappears exactly when the user starts typing. There is no `aria-invalid`, so assistive tech cannot tell a failed field from an empty one. The message has no id and nothing references it, so it exists visually and nowhere else. And validating on every keystroke turns the field red while the address is still half-typed, which is both hostile and hard to announce sensibly.

The wiring is small: `const id = useId()`, a real `<label htmlFor={id}>`, and an `errorId` derived from it. The input gets `id={id}`, `aria-invalid={error ? true : undefined}` (undefined, not `false`, keeps the attribute out of the DOM when valid) and `aria-describedby={error ? errorId : undefined}`. Described-by is a space-separated list, so it composes with any persistent hint such as how the address will be used. The message element keeps `id={errorId}` and stays rendered while the error exists, because a reference to a missing element is a silent no-op.

Announcement: pick one primary path and say so. `role="alert"` on a node that mounts with the text announces on insertion and is right when the failure must interrupt; a persistent `role="status"` region that receives the text is quieter and survives text changes. If the same message is both described-by and a live region, some screen readers read it twice, so I would state that trade-off and keep described-by for the on-demand read plus a single live region for the change.

Timing is the decision the prompt hides: validate on blur and on submit, then re-validate on change only after the first failure, so a user who is fixing the error gets immediate feedback while a user who is still typing is left alone. In a fully controlled field that policy belongs to the owner, so I would expose an optional `error` prop as the escape hatch and default to the internal policy. Nothing in this flow moves focus; the caret is not mine to take. Finally I would run the keyboard pass out loud, Tab to the field, type, submit, hear the message once, and show two instances side by side to prove the ids do not collide.
rubric: Replaces the visual `<span>` with a real `<label htmlFor>` and stable `useId`-based ids for the input and the message.
Models validity explicitly, with `aria-invalid` only while invalid, and references the rendered message from the input.
Chooses and states a validation timing policy (blur/submit, re-check on change) instead of validating every keystroke.
Picks one deliberate announcement path and acknowledges the double-announcement risk of described-by plus a live region.
Preserves the controlled contract and demonstrates a keyboard/screen-reader pass with multiple instances and a cleared error.

scenarios.prompt: Machine-coding round (45 min). Users must reorder these steps with a mouse, a keyboard, and on touch. With a mouse it works only sometimes, and it never works without one. Keep row identity, add the accessible command path, and explain the two bugs you fix.
scenarios.modelAnswer:
Two bugs first. `key={index}` binds row identity to position, so after a move React rewrites the existing DOM nodes with different data, and any per-row state, transition, or focus the browser was holding now belongs to the wrong step. And the `<li>` never calls `preventDefault()` on `dragover`, which is what marks an element as a valid drop target; without it `drop` does not reliably fire, which is the works-only-sometimes symptom. Those are one-line fixes but they change the data model, so I do them together: `key={item.id}` and `move(id, delta)` finding the index by id, returning the same array unchanged when the target is out of range.

Then the real requirement. Reordering has to be a command, not a gesture: every row gets two native buttons, `Move up` and `Move down`, named with the item so a screen-reader user knows what moves, and disabled at the boundaries instead of wrapping silently. Those buttons call the same `move` the drag path calls, and they are also the touch path, because `draggable` does nothing on touch. Drag stays as an enhancement over a command that already works.

Focus is where candidates lose the round. After the state update I refocus explicitly: keep a ref map keyed by item id, and after the commit focus the same-direction button on the moved row. The trap is that the button often becomes `disabled` at the new boundary, and a focused disabled button blurs to `<body>`, so the fallback target is the row's other button or the row itself, never the document. A pending-focus value consumed after render handles both cases.

Finally the feedback: a polite live region that says where the item landed, for example `Moved 'Preheat oven' to position 2 of 6`. That is the whole confirmation a screen-reader user gets, and it closes the status-message obligation. I would also fix the handle semantics, keeping the glyph decorative with `aria-hidden` while a real button carries the name, and I would not reach for `aria-grabbed` or `aria-dropeffect`, which are deprecated. Demo order: mouse drag, keyboard-only move across a boundary, a touch tap, then one undo.
rubric: Swaps by stable item id and keys the list by id, so a move never rebinds rows to the wrong data.
Fixes the drop target with `preventDefault` on dragover, clears the drag source, or states the gesture is optional.
Adds native Move up/Move down buttons with item-specific names, disabled at the boundaries, calling the same move function.
Restores focus after the reorder, including the case where the focused button becomes disabled.
Announces the new position in a live region and demonstrates keyboard-only and touch-only flows.
